title: AI and SQL
answer: Artificial intelligence runs on data, and most of the data that matters to a business sits in SQL databases. This section covers how AI reads those databases, writes queries against them, searches inside them and is kept from misusing them.

children.name: Text to SQL
children.blurb: Turning a question asked in plain English into a database query that answers it, the most direct way AI puts a company's own data in front of people who cannot write SQL.

children.name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
children.blurb: How the accuracy of AI generated SQL is measured, and why a high score on a public benchmark does not mean a model will answer correctly against a company's own messy schema.

children.name: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
children.blurb: How similarity search, the retrieval step behind AI assistants, now runs inside ordinary relational databases through extensions such as pgvector for PostgreSQL.

children.name: SQL and AI Training Data Pipelines
children.blurb: Where the data that trains and tunes models comes from inside a business: extract, transform and load jobs, much of it written in SQL, that decide what a model ever gets to see.

children.name: Feature Stores
children.blurb: The tables that hold the inputs a machine learning model reads, kept consistent so a model is trained and run on the same definition of each value.

children.name: Warehouses and Lakehouses for AI
children.blurb: The analytics platforms, data warehouses and lakehouses, where companies keep the history AI models are trained on and increasingly run AI functions directly next to the data.

children.name: Semantic Layers
children.blurb: A business meaning for raw tables, what revenue or an active customer actually means, which AI needs in order to write queries that answer the question a person actually asked.

children.name: SQL Injection Through AI
children.blurb: When a model writes the query, the old attack moves: text hidden in a question, a document or a web page can steer an AI into running a query nobody intended.

children.name: Agent Database Access and Permissions
children.blurb: What an AI agent is allowed to read and change in a database, and how row level security and least privilege keep it inside the same limits as the person it acts for.

children.name: MCP Database Servers
children.blurb: Model Context Protocol servers that connect AI assistants to SQL databases, the fastest growing way assistants reach company data, and the governance questions they raise.

children.name: AI Query Optimisation
children.blurb: Machine learning turned inward on the database itself: learned cost models, index advice and automatic tuning that make queries faster without a person rewriting them.

children.name: Data Quality for AI
children.blurb: Bad rows in, bad answers out: duplicates, stale records, missing values and silently changed definitions are among the most common reasons AI systems give wrong answers from correct code.

sections.body: A language model knows what it read during training. It does not know last quarter's sales, this morning's inventory or which customers renewed, because that information lives in a company's own databases, and most of those databases speak SQL. Every useful business answer an AI system gives about a company's own operations passes through a query at some point. That makes SQL less a programming skill and more the doorway between artificial intelligence and the facts it is supposed to be reasoning about.
sections.heading: Why SQL sits under AI

sections.body: The first is translation: text to SQL systems turn a plain English question into a query, so a manager can ask how many orders shipped late last month without waiting for an analyst. The second is retrieval: vector search now runs inside ordinary relational databases, so the documents an assistant searches can be filtered and permissioned like any other table. The third is action: AI agents and Model Context Protocol servers connect assistants directly to databases, and this site's MCP directory already lists more than 260 servers built for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and the cloud warehouses. Each of these puts a model one step closer to live data, which is where both the value and the risk come from.
sections.heading: Three ways AI now meets the database

sections.body: A query can be syntactically perfect and still answer the wrong question, because the model misunderstood what a column means or which table holds the truth. Generated SQL is also a new route for an old attack, since instructions hidden in a question or a document can steer a model into running a query nobody intended. And an agent with database credentials can quietly become a way around permissions that were designed for people. The controls that answer these problems are not new: least privilege, read only roles, row level security, reviewed queries, agreed business definitions and tests on the data itself. What is new is how much depends on applying them.
sections.heading: Where it goes wrong

sections.body: The pages start with the question most people bring, whether AI can reliably write SQL, through text to SQL and the benchmarks that measure it. They then move down into the data layer: vector search inside databases, the pipelines and feature stores that feed models, the warehouses and lakehouses that hold the history, and the semantic layers that give raw tables a business meaning. The last group covers control, SQL injection through AI, agent permissions, database MCP servers, AI tuning the database itself, and the data quality that decides whether any of it can be trusted. This site is its own example: every page here is built from a PostgreSQL database, and the pipeline that writes it is, underneath, a long series of SQL queries.
